headline: Joe-Pye Weed's Up, Bass Have Gone to Night Shift Below Essex
subhead: With the shad run a distant memory and the river running warm, the bass have slid into the dark hours — but the bluefish are still willing to show themselves in daylight off Great Island.
body_markdown:
The joe-pye weed is chest-high along the Great Island marsh edges now, that dusty pink bloom that tells you summer's settled in for good, and the young ospreys off Griswold Point are flying their own hunts, no longer waiting on mom to drop a bunker in the nest. That's where we are on this river — deep summer, the kind where the shad run feels like something you read about rather than something that happened four months ago. The alewives and the hickories are long gone upstream and out, and what's left in the current now is a different fishery altogether.

Water in the shallow flats off Great Island and up into North Cove has been running warm — into the mid-to-upper 70s on a sunny afternoon, no different from what the Sound stations are reading down at Kings Point and New London, roughly 69 to 71 out in open water. That's warm enough that the striped bass in this river have done what they do every July: gone nocturnal. I've said it before and I'll keep saying it because it holds up year after year — when the surface sits in the low-to-mid 70s, the bass you find rod-in-hand at two in the afternoon are the exception, not the rule. We flagged this pattern building last week and it's held exactly as expected — the daytime river has gone quiet, but after dark it wakes up.

If you want bass right now, you fish the dark hours off Saybrook Point — the breakwater and the outer bar where the river current collides with incoming Sound water. That collision is the whole game this time of year. On the outgoing tide, the river pushes out cooler, tannic water that rides up over the denser salt water from the Sound, and it creates a thermal seam right at the mouth that bass use like a highway. Eels fished on a fish-finder rig, slow-walked along that seam from an hour before high tide through the first few hours of the ebb, have been the most consistent producer I've heard of — fish in the 24 to 32-inch range, with the occasional better fish pushing 36. Bunker chunks fished on the bottom in 12 to 18 feet off the Point, same tide stage, have also been drawing bites, mostly after 9 or 10 at night once boat traffic clears out.

During daylight, the bass that are around are holding deep and tight to structure — the drop-off at Ferry Point, the pilings and scour holes around the Baldwin Bridge, and the deeper bends up toward Essex where the channel drops to 20-plus feet. A bucktail dragged slow along the bottom through those areas on the last two hours of the ebb has picked at a few fish, but it's been a grind — more blanks than bites, and I won't pretend otherwise. If you're only fishing daylight hours right now, set your expectations accordingly and treat any bass as a bonus.

Bluefish have been the more honest daytime player. They're following bunker schools that have pushed up into the lower river and along the flats off Great Island, and unlike the bass they haven't gone shy about showing themselves — you can see the nervous water and the occasional slash on the surface mid-morning and again in the last hour of daylight. Working topwater plugs or diamond jigs through those bunker pods on a moving tide has been good for choppers in the 3 to 6-pound range, with the odd bigger fish mixed in. That bluefish push matches what's been building up and down the coast this month — bunker-driven blitzes spreading both south and north — and the lower river's version of it has been reliable enough that I'd call it the surer bet for anyone who wants action they can see rather than fish blind for after dark.

For those who'd rather skip the night shift altogether, white perch have been steady in the deeper coves — North Cove, the water off DEP Marina, and the bends up past Essex. Small jigs tipped with bloodworms, fished slow along bottom in 8 to 15 feet on the last of the incoming, have been filling out a lot of quieter mornings. It's not glamorous fishing, but it's honest, and the perch have been cooperative all month.

Looking ahead, the moon's waxing toward full in early August, which means stronger tidal current building through the river mouth over the next week or two. That should sharpen both patterns — a harder-running outgoing tide will pull more bait and more bass through that thermal seam off Saybrook Point after dark, and stronger current should keep the bunker schools moving and the bluefish on them through the daylight hours off Great Island. If I had one evening to fish this week, I'd be on the outer bar an hour before high, eel in hand, waiting on that seam to load up as the ebb takes hold. Bring bug spray. The no-see-ums out on that flat this time of year are as reliable as anything else on this river.
